The **World Happiness Report** is a publication that contains articles and rankings of [national happiness](Gross_National_Happiness "Gross National Happiness"), based on respondent ratings of their own lives,[[1]](World_Happiness_Report#cite_note-1) which the report also correlates with various [(quality of) life](Quality_of_life "Quality of life") factors.[[2]](World_Happiness_Report#cite_note-auto-2) As of March 2023, <Finland> has been ranked the happiest country in the world six times in a row.[[3]](World_Happiness_Report#cite_note-NYT-20180314-3)[[4]](World_Happiness_Report#cite_note-USN-20180314-4)[[5]](World_Happiness_Report#cite_note-5)[[6]](World_Happiness_Report#cite_note-6)

The report is a publication of the [Sustainable Development Solutions Network](Sustainable_Development_Solutions_Network "Sustainable Development Solutions Network"), a global initiative of the [United Nations](United_Nations "United Nations").[[7]](World_Happiness_Report#cite_note-7) The report primarily uses data from the [Gallup World Poll](Gallup_(company) "Gallup (company)"). Each annual report is available to the public to download on the World Happiness Report website.[[2]](World_Happiness_Report#cite_note-auto-2) The Editors of the 2020 report are [John F. Helliwell](John_F._Helliwell "John F. Helliwell"), [Richard Layard](Richard_Layard "Richard Layard"), [Jeffrey D. Sachs](Jeffrey_D._Sachs "Jeffrey D. Sachs"), and [Jan-Emmanuel De Neve](Jan-Emmanuel_De_Neve "Jan-Emmanuel De Neve"). Associate Editors are [Lara Aknin](Lara_Aknin "Lara Aknin"), Shun Wang, and Haifang Huang.

## History

In July 2011, the [UN General Assembly](UN_General_Assembly "UN General Assembly") adopted resolution 65/309 *Happiness: Towards a Holistic Definition of Development*[[8]](World_Happiness_Report#cite_note-8) inviting member countries to measure the happiness of their people and to use the data to help guide public policy. On April 2, 2012, this was followed by the first UN High Level Meeting called *Wellbeing and Happiness: Defining a New Economic Paradigm*,[[9]](World_Happiness_Report#cite_note-9) which was chaired by UN Secretary General [Ban Ki-moon](Ban_Ki-moon "Ban Ki-moon") and Prime Minister [Jigmi Thinley](Jigmi_Thinley "Jigmi Thinley") of <Bhutan>, a nation that adopted [gross national happiness](Gross_national_happiness "Gross national happiness") instead of [gross domestic product](Gross_domestic_product "Gross domestic product") as their main development indicator.[[10]](World_Happiness_Report#cite_note-10)

The first World Happiness Report was released on April 1, 2012 as a foundational text for the UN *High Level Meeting: Well-being and Happiness: Defining a New Economic Paradigm*,[[11]](World_Happiness_Report#cite_note-11) drawing international attention.[[12]](World_Happiness_Report#cite_note-12) The first report outlined the state of world happiness, causes of happiness and misery, and policy implications highlighted by case studies. In 2013, the second World Happiness Report was issued, and in 2015 the third. Since 2016, it has been issued on an annual basis on the 20th of March, to coincide with the UN's International Day of Happiness.[[13]](World_Happiness_Report#cite_note-13)

## Methods and philosophy

The rankings of national [happiness](Happiness "Happiness") are based on a [Cantril ladder](Happiness#Measurement "Happiness") survey undertaken world-wide by the [polling](Opinion_poll "Opinion poll") company [Gallup, Inc](Gallup%2C_Inc "Gallup, Inc"). Nationally representative samples of respondents are asked to think of a ladder, with the best possible life for them being a 10, and the worst possible life being a 0. They are then asked to rate their own current lives on that 0 to 10 scale.[[14]](World_Happiness_Report#cite_note-auto1-14) The report correlates the life evaluation results with various life factors.[[2]](World_Happiness_Report#cite_note-auto-2)

The life factor variables used in the reports are reflective of determinants that explain national-level differences in life evaluations across research literature. However, certain variables, such as unemployment or inequality, are not considered because comparable data is not yet available across all countries. The variables used illustrate important correlations rather than causal estimates.[[14]](World_Happiness_Report#cite_note-auto1-14)

<Finland> has a population of over 5.6 million people and an average population density of 19 inhabitants per square kilometre (49/sq mi). This makes it the third most sparsely populated country in Europe, after Iceland and Norway. Population distribution is very uneven: the population is concentrated on the small southwestern coastal plain. About 85% live in towns and cities, with 1.5 million living in the [Greater Helsinki](Greater_Helsinki "Greater Helsinki") area.[[2]](Demographics_of_Finland#cite_note-ANNUAL2012-2) In Arctic Lapland, on the other hand, there are only two inhabitants per square kilometre (5.2/sq mi).

Finland is a relatively ethnically homogeneous country. The dominant ethnicity is [Finnish](Finns "Finns") but there are also notable historic minorities of [Finland-Swedes](Swedish-speaking_population_of_Finland "Swedish-speaking population of Finland"), [Sami](Sami_people "Sami people") and [Roma people](Finnish_Kale "Finnish Kale"). As a result of recent immigration there are now also large groups of ethnic [Russians](Russians_in_Finland "Russians in Finland"), [Estonians](Estonians_in_Finland "Estonians in Finland"), [Iraqis](Iraqis_in_Finland "Iraqis in Finland") and [Somalis](Somalis_in_Finland "Somalis in Finland") in the country. 8.9% of the population is born abroad and 5.8% are foreign citizens.[[3]](Demographics_of_Finland#cite_note-:1-3) The official languages are [Finnish](Finnish_language "Finnish language") and [Swedish](Swedish_language "Swedish language"), the latter being the native language of about 5.2% of the Finnish population.[[4]](Demographics_of_Finland#cite_note-Statfi-4) From the 13th to the early 19th century Finland was a part of <Sweden>.

With 65.2% of Finns in its congregation, the [Lutheran Church](Evangelical_Lutheran_Church_of_Finland "Evangelical Lutheran Church of Finland") is the largest religious group in the country. Two million people with roots in Finland live abroad. In a 2017 survey, 10% of residents of Finland said that they would prefer to live abroad.[[5]](Demographics_of_Finland#cite_note-5)
